string.name: isWellFormed
string.documentation:
Tests whether text contains a valid Unicode representation. Takes no arguments; every native UTF-8 string returns true.

```tsrust
console.log("é😊".isWellFormed()); // prints "true"
```

Lone surrogate strings cannot be constructed in Tsrust. Receiver is borrowed and unchanged.

string.name: toWellFormed
string.documentation:
Returns unchanged string content. Takes no arguments and leaves the receiver reusable.

```tsrust
console.log("Hello".toWellFormed()); // prints "Hello"
```

Native strings are always valid UTF-8 and cannot contain lone surrogates. No surrogate replacement is needed. Static text can remain borrowed; owned text receives an independent copy.

string.name: trim
string.documentation:
Removes whitespace from both ends, preserving interior whitespace and returning a string without changing the receiver. Takes no arguments.

```tsrust
console.log("  Hello  ".trim()); // prints "Hello"
```

Whitespace includes Unicode whitespace: U+0085 is removed, while U+FEFF is preserved. Static text can retain a borrowed slice; owned input produces an independent copy.

string.name: trimStart
string.documentation:
Removes whitespace from the beginning, preserving interior whitespace and returning a string without changing the receiver. Takes no arguments.

```tsrust
console.log("  Hello  ".trimStart()); // prints "Hello  "
```

Whitespace includes Unicode whitespace: U+0085 is removed, while U+FEFF is preserved. Static text can retain a borrowed slice; owned input produces an independent copy.

string.name: trimEnd
string.documentation:
Removes whitespace from the end, preserving interior whitespace and returning a string without changing the receiver. Takes no arguments.

```tsrust
console.log("  Hello  ".trimEnd()); // prints "  Hello"
```

Whitespace includes Unicode whitespace: U+0085 is removed, while U+FEFF is preserved. Static text can retain a borrowed slice; owned input produces an independent copy.

string.name: trimLeft
string.documentation:
Removes whitespace from the beginning, preserving interior whitespace and returning a string without changing the receiver. Takes no arguments.

```tsrust
console.log("  Hello  ".trimLeft()); // prints "Hello  "
```

string.name: trimRight
string.documentation:

```tsrust

```

Whitespace includes Unicode whitespace: U+0085 is removed, while U+FEFF is preserved. Static text can retain a borrowed slice; owned input produces an independent copy. Alias of trimEnd().

string.name: toLowerCase
string.documentation:
Converts text to lowercase using Unicode case mappings. Takes no arguments and leaves the original unchanged.

```tsrust
console.log("ÉCOLE".toLowerCase()); // prints "école"
```

Locale-independent conversion may expand characters and change byte length. The receiver is borrowed; the result owns its text.

string.name: toUpperCase
string.documentation:
Converts text to uppercase using Unicode case mappings. Takes no arguments and leaves the original unchanged.

```tsrust
console.log("Straße".toUpperCase()); // prints "STRASSE"
```

Locale-independent conversion may expand characters and change byte length. The receiver is borrowed; the result owns its text.

string.name: toLocaleLowerCase
string.documentation:
Returns the string converted to lowercase. The result is the same as `toLowerCase()`.

Takes no arguments. A locale argument such as `"tr"` is an `unsupported` error, because locale-specific rules are not provided; the conversion always uses the general Unicode mapping, whatever the system language is.

@returns A new string. A character can change length: `"İ"` becomes `i` followed by a combining dot.

```tsrust
console.log("ÉCOLE Straße".toLocaleLowerCase()); // prints "école straße"
```

Text in Turkish, Azerbaijani or Lithuanian can need rules that this conversion does not apply, for example dotted and dotless i.

The receiver is only read. The result is a new owned string.

string.name: toLocaleUpperCase
string.documentation:
Returns the string converted to uppercase. The result is the same as `toUpperCase()`.

Takes no arguments. A locale argument such as `"tr"` is an `unsupported` error, because locale-specific rules are not provided; the conversion always uses the general Unicode mapping, whatever the system language is.

@returns A new string. A character can change length: `"ß"` becomes `"SS"`.

```tsrust
console.log("école straße".toLocaleUpperCase()); // prints "ÉCOLE STRASSE"
```

Text in Turkish, Azerbaijani or Lithuanian can need rules that this conversion does not apply, for example dotted and dotless i.

The receiver is only read. The result is a new owned string.

string.name: includes
string.signature: includes(search: string | StringView | JsonValue | JsonView, position?: int): boolean
string.documentation:
Tests whether search text occurs anywhere in the receiver. Optional position clamps to [0, byte length], default zero (start of the searched suffix). The search argument is a string; the receiver remains unchanged.

@param search - Text to find; matched literally, without regular expressions or Unicode normalization.
@param position - UTF-8 byte boundary, clamped to the string bounds; defaults to zero.

```tsrust
console.log("hello".includes("ell")); // prints "true"
```

Search coordinates use UTF-8 bytes, not UTF-16 units. Explicit search boundaries must be valid scalar boundaries. String operands are borrowed.

A StringView supports this read directly. A JsonValue or JsonView proven to contain a string by a stable typeof guard also supports this read without copying or consuming its text. The search argument may also be a JSON value proven to contain a string. The source owner stays borrowed for the complete operation; later arguments cannot invalidate it.

string.signature: startsWith(search: string | StringView | JsonValue | JsonView, position?: int): boolean
string.documentation:

@param search - Text to find; matched literally, without regular expressions or Unicode normalization.
@param position - UTF-8 byte boundary, clamped to the string bounds; defaults to zero.

```tsrust

```

A StringView supports this read directly. A JsonValue or JsonView proven to contain a string by a stable typeof guard also supports this read without copying or consuming its text. string.name: indexOf
string.signature: indexOf(search: string | StringView | JsonValue | JsonView, fromIndex?: int): int
string.documentation:
Returns the first matching byte offset, or -1 when absent. The search argument is a string; the receiver remains unchanged.

@param search - Text to find; matched literally, without regular expressions or Unicode normalization.
@param fromIndex - Byte offset; negative values clamp to zero, large values clamp to byte length. Defaults to zero.

```tsrust
console.log("éclair".indexOf("c")); // prints "2"
```

fromIndex defaults to zero. Search coordinates use UTF-8 bytes, not UTF-16 units. Explicit search boundaries must be valid scalar boundaries. String operands are borrowed.

A StringView supports this read directly. A JsonValue or JsonView proven to contain a string by a stable typeof guard also supports this read without copying or consuming its text. The search argument may also be a JSON value proven to contain a string. The source owner stays borrowed for the complete operation; later arguments cannot invalidate it.

string.signature: lastIndexOf(search: string | StringView | JsonValue | JsonView, fromIndex?: int): int
string.documentation:

```tsrust

```

string.name: slice
string.documentation:
Returns the portion between start (inclusive) and end (exclusive). Both are optional integer byte offsets; defaults are zero and byte length. Negative offsets count from the end; bounds clamp to the string. Reversed bounds return empty text.

@param start - UTF-8 byte start offset. Negative values count from the end; bounds clamp. Defaults to zero.
@param end - Exclusive UTF-8 byte bound, default byte length. Negative values count from the end and bounds clamp.

```tsrust
console.log("hello".slice(1, 4)); // prints "ell"
```

Nonempty endpoints must be UTF-8 scalar boundaries. The receiver is borrowed; static slices may stay borrowed, owned slices copy.

string.name: substring
string.documentation:
Returns text between two clamped byte offsets. start is required; end defaults to byte length. Negative offsets clamp to zero and reversed bounds swap.

@param start - UTF-8 byte start offset. Required; negative bounds clamp to zero. Required.
@param end - Exclusive UTF-8 byte bound, default byte length. Reversed bounds swap; negative bounds clamp to zero.

```tsrust
console.log("hello".substring(4, 1)); // prints "ell"
```

Nonempty endpoints must be UTF-8 scalar boundaries; empty ranges skip boundary checks. Static slices can stay borrowed; owned results copy.

string.name: substr
string.documentation:
Returns up to length bytes of text beginning at start, without changing the receiver. Both arguments are optional ints. start defaults to zero; a negative start counts from the end, then clamps to [0, byte length]. length defaults to the remaining bytes. A length <= 0 returns empty text, and a positive length is capped at the remaining bytes without overflowing. All signed 64-bit int values are accepted for these bounds. More than two arguments or arguments of other types are errors; no coercion is performed. The receiver and supplied arguments are evaluated once, left to right, even for an empty or full result.

@param start - Optional signed int UTF-8 byte start, default zero. Negative values count from the end; the resulting offset clamps to the string bounds.
@param length - Optional int byte count, default remaining bytes. Values <= 0 give empty text; positive values cap at the remaining bytes without overflow.

```tsrust
console.log("hello".substr(1, 3)); // prints "ell"
console.log("hello".substr(-3, 2)); // prints "ll"
console.log("é😀x".substr(2, 4)); // prints "😀"
console.log("é".substr(1, 0)); // prints empty text
```

Bounds count UTF-8 bytes, unlike the legacy JavaScript substr method's UTF-16 code units. Both endpoints of a nonempty result must be Unicode scalar boundaries; otherwise execution fails with a source-located boundary diagnostic. For example, "é".substr(1, 1) fails because byte 1 is inside é, and "😀".substr(0, 1) fails because the end is inside the astral scalar. Empty ranges skip these checks. On "hello", start -9223372036854775808 clamps to zero, start 9223372036854775807 gives empty text, and length 9223372036854775807 returns only the remaining bytes.

The receiver is borrowed through argument evaluation and remains reusable; later arguments cannot move or mutate that borrowed input. Empty results use static empty text. A full nonempty range uses Cow cloning: static text can be shared, while owned text is independently copied. Partial static text can borrow a static slice; partial owned text is independently copied.

examples.source: const text = "hello".repeat(1); const piece = text.substr(1, 3); console.log(piece); console.log(text);

string.name: charAt
string.documentation:
Returns the Unicode scalar at an integer index, default zero. Negative or out-of-range indices return empty text.

@param index - Unicode scalar index, default zero; outside the string returns empty text.

```tsrust
console.log("é😊".charAt(1)); // prints "😊"
```

Counts Unicode scalars, unlike byte-indexed slice and JavaScript UTF-16 charAt. Receiver is borrowed; a selected scalar produces owned text.

string.name: concat
string.documentation:
Appends zero or more string arguments in order and returns the combined text. No coercion is performed; the receiver is unchanged.

@param values - Strings appended in order, without coercion.

```tsrust
console.log("Hello".concat(" ", "world")); // prints "Hello world"
```

Operands are borrowed. Changed text owns an independent buffer; zero/all-empty arguments clone the receiver with static sharing or an owned copy.

Spread arguments may come from strings, arrays or Sets whose elements are strings. String sources construct Unicode scalar character values and stay usable.

```tsrust
console.log("a".concat(..."bc"));
// prints abc
```

string.name: padStart
string.documentation:
Pads the beginning until the integer target byte length is reached. Optional filler defaults to a space and repeats as needed. Short/negative targets or empty filler leave text unchanged.

@param target - Destination byte length of the padded string; short or negative targets leave it unchanged.
@param filler - String repeated to fill missing bytes; defaults to one space, empty text disables padding.

```tsrust
console.log("7".padStart(3, "0")); // prints "007"
```

Targets count UTF-8 bytes, not JavaScript UTF-16 units. A truncated filler must end at a scalar boundary or fail. Receiver stays reusable; changed results own their storage, no-ops use Cow cloning.

string.name: padEnd
string.documentation:
Pads the end until the integer target byte length is reached. Optional filler defaults to a space and repeats as needed. Short/negative targets or empty filler leave text unchanged.

@param target - Destination byte length of the padded string; short or negative targets leave it unchanged.
@param filler - String repeated to fill missing bytes; defaults to one space, empty text disables padding.

```tsrust
console.log("7".padEnd(3, "0")); // prints "700"
```

Targets count UTF-8 bytes, not JavaScript UTF-16 units. A truncated filler must end at a scalar boundary or fail. Receiver stays reusable; changed results own their storage, no-ops use Cow cloning.

string.name: repeat
string.documentation:
Repeats the receiver count times, returning new text. count is a required nonnegative integer; zero produces empty text. Negative counts and excessive lengths fail.

@param count - Nonnegative integer repetition count; zero returns empty text.

```tsrust
console.log("ha".repeat(3)); // prints "hahaha"
```

Receiver is borrowed; output has independent storage.

string.name: replace
string.documentation:
Replaces the first occurrence of string search with replacement text. The original remains unchanged. Regular expressions are unsupported.

@param search - Text to find; matched literally, without regular expressions or Unicode normalization.
@param replacement - Replacement text; supports $$, $&, $` and $' templates.

```tsrust
console.log("banana".replace("a", "o")); // prints "bonana"
```

Replacement templates support $$ (literal dollar), $& (match), $` (prefix) and $' (suffix); capture references have no regex groups. Operands are borrowed; output owns its text.

string.name: replaceAll
string.documentation:
Replaces every non-overlapping occurrence of string search with replacement text. The original remains unchanged. Regular expressions are unsupported.

@param search - Text to find; matched literally, without regular expressions or Unicode normalization.
@param replacement - Replacement text; supports $$, $&, $` and $' templates.

```tsrust
console.log("banana".replaceAll("a", "o")); // prints "bonono"
```

Replacement templates support $$ (literal dollar), $& (match), $` (prefix) and $' (suffix); capture references have no regex groups. Operands are borrowed; output owns its text.

string.name: split
string.documentation:
Returns a string array by splitting the receiver at a literal string separator. The receiver is unchanged. The optional separator must be a string; when omitted, the result contains the whole receiver as one element, including an empty receiver. The optional limit must be an int. It is converted modulo 2^32 to an unsigned count from 0 through 4294967295; omission defaults to 4294967295. A converted count of zero returns an empty array. Other counts keep only the first pieces and discard the rest; the remainder is not joined into the last piece. More than two arguments or other argument types are errors. Receiver and supplied arguments are evaluated once, left to right, even when the converted limit is zero.

@param separator - Optional literal string separator. Omission returns the whole text as one element. Empty text splits Unicode scalar values, without artificial leading or trailing empty pieces.
@param limit - Optional int converted modulo 2^32 to the maximum number of returned pieces. Defaults to 4294967295; -1 converts to that same count, 4294967296 converts to zero, and 4294967297 converts to one. Pieces beyond the converted cap are discarded.

```tsrust
const parts = "a,b,c".split(",", 2);
console.log(parts.length); // prints "2"
console.log(parts[1]); // prints "b", not "b,c"
console.log("😀é".split("").length); // prints "2"
console.log("".split("").length); // prints "0"
console.log("".split().length); // prints "1"
console.log("a,b".split(",", -1).length); // prints "2"
console.log("a,b".split(",", 4294967296).length); // prints "0"
```

Nonempty separators match literally and do not overlap. Leading, adjacent and trailing separators retain empty pieces: "a,,".split(",") has three elements. Empty separators split Unicode scalars, including separate combining marks, rather than JavaScript UTF-16 code units. Limit wrapping preserves the existing unsigned 32-bit count contract: -1 permits up to 4294967295 pieces, while 4294967296 permits none. All signed int limit values are accepted; no implicit numeric or string coercion is performed. Regular expressions, omitted-argument placeholders and argument coercion are unsupported.

The receiver and separator are borrowed through argument evaluation; later arguments cannot move or mutate an earlier borrowed operand. The returned array is independent. Pieces from static text may borrow static slices; pieces from owned input have independent copied storage. An omitted separator uses the ordinary Cow clone of the receiver.

examples.source: const parts = "😀é".split(""); console.log(parts.length); console.log(parts[0]); console.log(parts[1]); console.log("e\u0301".split("").length);

console.log("".split("").length); console.log("".split().length); console.log("a,b".split(",", -1).length); console.log("a,b".split(",", 0).length); console.log("a,b".split(",", 4294967296).length); console.log("a,b".split(",", 4294967297).length);
const text = "a,b".repeat(1); const parts = text.split(); console.log(parts[0]); console.log(text);

string.name: anchor
string.documentation: Returns the receiver text inside and tags. Requires exactly one string argument, name, used as the name attribute. Only ASCII double quotes in that attribute are replaced with "; ampersands, angle brackets and single quotes are unchanged. Missing, extra or non-string arguments are errors. No implicit coercion or default "undefined" attribute is supplied. The receiver remains unchanged. The raw receiver content is inserted without escaping; this method is not an HTML sanitizer. @param name - Required string anchor name; only ASCII double quotes become ". No value validation or coercion is performed. ```tsrust console.log("hello".anchor("section")); // prints "hello" ``` For a quote-containing attribute, "é😀".anchor("a\"&<>'") returns "'\">é😀". This is a legacy, deprecated JavaScript HTML-wrapper method. Native strings are valid UTF-8; Unicode text is preserved exactly. Strict string types replace JavaScript argument coercion. No DOM operation, rendering, URL validation or HTML sanitization occurs. The receiver and attribute are borrowed and evaluated once, left to right, remaining reusable. Later arguments cannot move or mutate the borrowed receiver. Every result is a fresh, independently owned string, including an empty receiver.


string.name: at
string.documentation:
Returns the character at a position counted from the start, or from the end when the position is negative.

@param index - Required int position. `0` is the first character and `-1` is the last. Positions count whole Unicode characters, so an accented letter or an emoji is one position.

```tsrust
const text="aé😀b";console.log(String(text.at(0)),String(text.at(-1)),String(text.at(2))); // prints "a b 😀"
```

```tsrust
const text="ab";console.log(String(text.at(2)),text.at(5)??"none"); // prints "undefined none"
```

Receiver is borrowed and unchanged; the returned character is a new string owned by the caller.

NFKC and NFKD also replace compatibility characters, such as ligatures and circled digits, with their ordinary equivalents.

```tsrust

```

```tsrust

```

```tsrust
const values:int[][]=[[1,2],[],[3]];

```

```tsrust
const values:null[]=[null,null];

```

Standard native digits may differ at rounding boundaries. Custom overrides, prototype hooks and boxed values are absent. This method belongs to arrays; Number.toString is unsupported.

The receiver is borrowed and evaluated once, remains reusable, and produces one independently owned string.

Array.name: join
Array.documentation:


```tsrust

```

Integers retain their full signed 64-bit decimal values; finite Number magnitudes from 1e-6 inclusive to 1e21 exclusive use ordinary decimal notation, with scientific notation outside that range and an explicit sign on the exponent. Array.name: some
Array.signature: some(callback: (value: Element, index: int, source: Element[]) => boolean): boolean
parameters: callback: (value: Element, index: int, source: Element[]) => boolean
Array.documentation:

@param callback - Reusable callback with optional element, index and source arguments; must return boolean.

A zero-parameter callback can observe a callable array without taking its environments; reusable and once elements stay available afterward. Stored reusable callable elements can be lent to an arrow visitor directly, through a local binding or from a factory. Use a mutate callable element parameter, followed by an optional int index. Ownership: the receiver is borrowed for the iteration and is not cloned or consumed. The result does not copy receiver elements.

An arrow visitor can be supplied directly, held in a local binding or returned by a factory; forwarded function declarations and abstract visitor parameters are not yet supported.

For data-element callbacks, additional trailing optional or defaulted parameters receive undefined. A default initializer runs for each reached callback invocation when its supplied value is undefined; a present null does not trigger it. // true

The supplied data tuple is element, index and source. Owned element and source-array arguments remain borrowed and cannot transfer into a rest pack. Data elements are borrowed for each invocation. The accumulator follows its declared access: it may be read, mutated or transferred; returning an independent owned value transfers it into the next step. The receiver is not reordered.

For an array of reusable callable environments, supply an independent initialValue and an arrow visitor taking an accumulator, a mutate callable element, and optionally an int index. Each visited environment is borrowed exclusively; captured-state changes remain available afterward. Array.name: pop
Array.documentation:
Removes and returns the last element of a supported dense homogeneous array. Takes no arguments; supplying any argument is an arity error. An empty array returns undefined and remains empty. Otherwise length decreases by one. Returns the element type or undefined; duplicate undefined alternatives collapse. The receiver remains available with its remaining elements.

```tsrust
let values:int[]=[1,2,3];const removed=values.pop();console.log(String(removed),values.length,values.join("|")); // 3 2 1|2
let empty:int[]=[];console.log(String(empty.pop()),empty.length);empty.push(7);console.log(String(empty.pop()),String(empty.pop()),empty.length);
// undefined 0
// 7 undefined 0
```

Supports existing homogeneous scalar, nested-array and record element types. Sparse arrays and prototype overrides are unsupported; mixed or nullable elements need a declared union element type such as `(int | string)[]`. Number results retain their original IEEE bits, including signed zero and NaN. An undefined[] element is indistinguishable from an empty removal result; the changed length distinguishes the cases. Nullable array receivers and returned payloads require a strict null/undefined guard before member access.

Requires mutable access to the receiver. Removed owned strings, arrays and records transfer into the result without cloning; no reference to the removed slot is returned. Remaining elements and the receiver keep their owners.

Use postfix `!` when an element must be present: `const users=["Pat"]; const user=users.pop()!; console.log(user.toUpperCase());` prints `PAT` and gives `user` type `string`. If the array is empty, the assertion fails at runtime with a non-null assertion message. Use `??` for a fallback instead.

Ownership: `!` does not clone or change transfer/borrow rules; the removed owned element remains an owned result.

For a fallback on any falsy result, use `||`: `const users=["Alice"]; const name=users.pop() || "Guest"; console.log(name);` prints `Alice` and gives `name` type `string`. An empty string also selects `"Guest"`. Use `??` to preserve an empty string and replace only null/undefined. Both operators evaluate the left operand once and skip the fallback when it is not needed.

Ownership: an owning logical result transfers selected owned values; readonly inspection borrows them. No implicit clone is added.

A standalone removal statement drops its result there. For a known dense local array, this releases captures belonging only to the removed callback. A discarded comma sequence containing direct removals and scalar operations also drops each removal result before its next operand; for example, `(handlers.pop(), second[0] = 9)` permits the assignment when only the removed element captured second. Nested discarded comma sequences preserve this order. A local declaration can retain a direct final removal: `const removed = (handlers.pop(), second[0] = 9, handlers.shift())` drops the discarded pop result before the assignment and transfers the final shift result into removed. Its captures stay protected until removed is disposed or replaced. A separately declared local `Holder | undefined` slot may start as `undefined` and later receive a concrete removal result; `Holder | null` slots similarly support `null`. Direct named reassignment of an existing concrete removal result can use the same final-removal form. The previous result stays alive while all RHS operands run and is dropped only after the new result has been evaluated; only then do its unshared captures become available. A removal result passed to another function remains protected during evaluation of the other arguments. Surviving elements and retained results keep their own captures protected. For a direct removal from a known dense local array, a local result owns only the removed element’s captures; leaving its lexical scope releases those captures. Direct result replacement in a normal lexical sequence evaluates the new value first, then drops the previous value and releases captures with no remaining owner. Replacements with a different captured environment inside branches or loops are not supported yet. Uncertain array contents retain conservative protection.

```tsrust
type Holder={run:ReadOnly<Function<int>>;};function main():void{const first=[3];const second=[5];const handlers:Holder[]=[{run:():int=>first[0]},{run:():int=>second[0]}];handlers.pop();second[0]=9;console.log(handlers[0].run(),second[0]);}
// 3 9
```

Array.name: entries
keys
Array.documentation:
Returns the index of every element, in order: `0`, `1`, up to `length - 1`. Takes no arguments. An empty array gives an empty result.

```tsrust
const words=["a","b","c"];console.log(words.keys().join(",")); // prints "0,1,2"
```

```tsrust
const words=["a","b"];let total=0;for(const index of words.keys()){total+=index;}const empty:int[]=[];console.log(total,empty.keys().length); // prints "1 0"
```

The result is an ordinary `int[]`, so it works in `for...of`, with `Array.from`, in array spread and with every array method. Passing an argument is an `arity` error. It is a new array computed when called; it does not follow later changes to the receiver, and there is no iterator object with a `next()` method.

Receiver is borrowed and unchanged; the returned array is owned by the caller.

examples.source: const words=["a","b"];let total=0;for(const index of words.keys()){total+=index;}const empty:int[]=[];console.log(total,empty.keys().length);

Array.name: values
Array.documentation:
Returns the elements in order as a new array. Takes no arguments. An empty array gives an empty result.

```tsrust
const words=["a","b"];const copy=words.values();copy[0]="changed";console.log(words.join(","),copy.join(",")); // prints "a,b changed,b"
```

```tsrust
let total=0;for(const value of [1,2,3].values()){total+=value;}console.log(total); // prints "6"
```

The result is an ordinary array of the same element type, so it works in `for...of`, with `Array.from`, in array spread and with every array method. Passing an argument is an `arity` error. It is an independent copy made when called: changing it never changes the receiver, it does not follow later changes to the receiver, and there is no iterator object with a `next()` method.

Receiver is borrowed and unchanged; owned elements such as strings and records are copied into the returned array.

Array.name: toLocaleString
Array.documentation:
Formats every array element as text and separates consecutive elements with commas. Takes no arguments. The receiver is unchanged and the result is a new string.

Numbers use comma groups of three integer digits, a period decimal separator and up to three fractional places. Decimal ties round away from zero; trailing fractional zeros are removed. Negative zero stays `-0`; infinities use `∞` and `-∞`. Integers retain their full signed 64-bit range. These rules are fixed and do not depend on the system language.

Strings keep their text, booleans give `true` or `false`, and records give `[object Object]`. Null and undefined elements contribute empty text while retaining their separators. Empty arrays give `""`. Nested arrays use the same rules recursively; their text is inserted without quotes or brackets.

```tsrust
const values:number[]=[1000.5,-0.0,1.2345];
console.log(values.toLocaleString()); // prints 1,000.5,-0,1.235
```

```tsrust
const values:int[][]=[[1000],[],[2000,3000]];
console.log(values.toLocaleString(),[null,null].toLocaleString()); // prints 1,000,,2,000,3,000 ,
```

Commas already inside an element or numeric grouping are not escaped, so the result is display text rather than a reversible serialization. Locale/options arguments and function-source elements are `unsupported` errors. Custom element formatting methods, other language rules and sparse arrays are unavailable. Text remains valid Unicode.

Ownership: the receiver and all nested elements are borrowed; they remain usable. The returned string owns its text.

Number.name: parseFloat
Number.documentation:
Parses the longest decimal prefix after leading ECMAScript whitespace. Accepts one string, optional sign, decimal fraction/exponent or Infinity. Incomplete exponents stop before the exponent; invalid starts return NaN.

@param text - Borrowed string to parse; a valid decimal/Infinity prefix is accepted despite trailing text.

```tsrust
console.log(Number.parseFloat("  1.25tail")); // prints "1.25"
```

Unlike Number(text), trailing text is permitted. Results use 64-bit floating-point precision; overflow produces Infinity, underflow can produce zero, and signed zero is preserved. Input is borrowed without a parsing buffer.

Number.name: parseInt
Number.documentation:
Reads a whole number from the start of a string and returns it as a number. Leading spaces are skipped, an optional `+` or `-` sign is accepted, and reading stops at the first character that is not a digit of the radix, so trailing text is ignored.

@param text - String to read. It is not changed.
@param radix - Optional int base from 2 through 36; letters `a` to `z` (either case) are digits above 9. When omitted or `0`, base 10 is used, or base 16 when the digits start with `0x` or `0X`. With radix 16 a `0x` prefix is also accepted.

Returns `NaN` when no digit can be read, for example an empty string, `"abc"` or `"0x"`, and when the radix is outside 2 through 36. A fraction is not read: `"3.9"` gives `3`.

```tsrust
console.log(Number.parseInt("42px"),Number.parseInt("  -17"),Number.parseInt("3.9")); // prints "42 -17 3"
```

```tsrust
console.log(Number.parseInt("ff",16),Number.parseInt("0x1F"),Number.parseInt("101",2)); // prints "255 31 5"
```

```tsrust
console.log(Number.parseInt("abc"),Number.parseInt("12",1),Number.isNaN(Number.parseInt(""))); // prints "NaN NaN true"
```

Calling it with no argument or more than two is an `arity` error. The first argument must be a string and the radix an int; a number radix such as `10.5` is a `type` error. The result is a `number`, not an `int`, because it can be `NaN`; assigning it to an `int` is a `type` error. Values beyond 9007199254740992 are rounded to the nearest representable number.

The string is borrowed for the call and stays usable; the result is a plain number.

JSON.name: parse

parameters.label: text: ReadOnly<string>
parameters.documentation: Required strict JSON document. UTF-8 byte length is bounded by maxBytes.

parameters.label: limits?: ReadOnly<JsonLimits>
parameters.documentation: Optional complete limits record. Omission uses the documented defaults; negative limits or maxDepth above 64 throw invalid-limits.

JSON.documentation:
Parses one strict JSON document and returns an independent JsonValue or throws a structured JsonError. text is UTF-8; leading and trailing JSON whitespace is allowed. Trailing non-whitespace, malformed syntax, invalid escapes, lone surrogates and nonfinite numbers reject. Duplicate object keys keep the last value and count toward maxEntries. Keys are sorted, integers within signed/unsigned 64-bit ranges remain exact, larger integers may round to finite floating point, and negative zero survives. Optional limits default to 16777216 bytes, 64 container levels, 1000000 entries per collection and 1000000 values. Budget failures have distinct codes; offset counts bytes, not characters. Neither argument changes. Catch errors with try/catch; JsonError retains code, message and byte offset. Uses checked JsonValue rather than dynamically typed objects. No reviver or replacer callback is supported.

With an explicit type argument, parse<T> validates and directly constructs T. Supports owned scalar values, records, tuples, arrays and recursive records with nullable or optional links. Required fields must exist; omitted optional fields become undefined. Unknown fields are skipped but still count against every input limit. Each occurrence of a known field must match its type; valid duplicate fields keep the last value. A shape mismatch produces shape-mismatch. int accepts integral values within signed 64-bit range; number rejects signed or unsigned 64-bit integer payloads that would lose precision. Larger integer tokens follow the finite floating-point parsing rules. Numeric failures use integer-range, integer-fractional or number-precision. Multiple non-null union alternatives, native resources and borrowed views other than JsonRaw are not typed decoding targets. Omitting <T> retains the JsonValue return contract. This is checked decoding, not a type assertion.

```tsrust
function main(){try{JSON.parse("null secret");}catch(error){console.log(error.code,error.offset);}}
```

Expected output: trailing-data 5. Ownership: borrows text and limits; results without JsonRaw own independent storage and can outlive the input. JsonRaw fields retain a borrow of text.

Raw fields: Explicit JsonRaw fields preserve the selected value's source tokens without constructing a dynamic subtree. Their source text must outlive every use; containing values cannot be cloned. Raw fields work in strict JSON typed decoding, including arrays and optional fields; JSONC and JSONL typed decoding still require owned fields. JSON.stringify and JSON.tryStringify preserve raw source text exactly; enclosing depth and output byte limits still apply.

Integer tokens without a decimal point or exponent are preserved exactly within signed 64-bit or unsigned 64-bit JSON storage. JSON.documentation:
Parses one strict JSON document and returns Ok with an independent JsonValue or Err with a structured JsonError. text is UTF-8; leading and trailing JSON whitespace is allowed. Trailing non-whitespace, malformed syntax, invalid escapes, lone surrogates and nonfinite numbers reject. Duplicate object keys keep the last value and count toward maxEntries. Keys are sorted, integers within signed/unsigned 64-bit ranges remain exact, larger integers may round to finite floating point, and negative zero survives. Optional limits default to 16777216 bytes, 64 container levels, 1000000 entries per collection and 1000000 values. Budget failures have distinct codes; offset counts bytes, not characters. Neither argument changes. Inspect the Result with match; malformed input or invalid limits do not throw JsonError. Uses checked JsonValue rather than dynamically typed objects. No reviver or replacer callback is supported.

With an explicit type argument, tryParse<T> validates and directly constructs T. Supports owned scalar values, records, tuples, arrays and recursive records with nullable or optional links. Required fields must exist; omitted optional fields become undefined. Unknown fields are skipped but still count against every input limit. Each occurrence of a known field must match its type; valid duplicate fields keep the last value. A shape mismatch produces shape-mismatch. int accepts integral values within signed 64-bit range; number rejects signed or unsigned 64-bit integer payloads that would lose precision. Larger integer tokens follow the finite floating-point parsing rules. Numeric failures use integer-range, integer-fractional or number-precision. Multiple non-null union alternatives, native resources and borrowed views other than JsonRaw are not typed decoding targets. Omitting <T> retains the JsonValue return contract. This is checked decoding, not a type assertion.

```tsrust
function main(){match(JSON.tryParse("null secret")){Ok(_)=>{throw "unexpected success";},Err(error)=>{console.log(error.code,error.offset);}}}
```

Raw fields: Explicit JsonRaw fields preserve the selected value's source tokens without constructing a dynamic subtree. Their source text must outlive every use; containing values cannot be cloned. Raw fields work in strict JSON typed decoding, including arrays and optional fields; JSONC and JSONL typed decoding still require owned fields. JSON.documentation:
Encodes scalars, named records, tuples, arrays and dynamic JSON values as strict JSON. Returns a UTF-8 string or throws JsonError. Ordinary object keys are sorted; tuples encode as arrays. The optional nonnegative maxBytes limit defaults to 16777216 bytes. Negative limits report invalid-limits; output exceeding the limit reports output-limit without returning partial output. Omits undefined object fields; root and array undefined report undefined-value. Nonfinite numbers report number-nonfinite. More than 64 nested containers reports depth-limit, including dynamic JSON nested inside typed records. Preserves exact int values and floating negative zero. Escapes quotes, backslashes and control characters; other Unicode remains UTF-8. Unsupported resources, collections and callbacks are rejected during checking. No replacer callback is supported. JSON.stringify and JSON.tryStringify preserve raw source text exactly, including whitespace, key order, escapes and number spelling. Raw fragments count toward the enclosing 64-container depth limit and output byte limit. JSONL writing preserves single-line raw text; literal CR or LF returns record-newline before writing any bytes of that record. Escaped newline sequences remain valid.


Expected output: {"count":42,"name":"hello"}.

Math.name: random
Math.documentation:
Returns a pseudo-random number that is at least 0 and less than 1. Every value in that range is about equally likely.

Takes no arguments; passing one is an `arity` error.

@returns A `number` from 0 (possible) up to but not including 1. The result is never an `int`.

```tsrust
const roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6.0) + 1.0;
console.log(roll >= 1.0 && roll <= 6.0, Math.random() < 1.0); // prints "true true"
```

Scale and shift the result for other ranges: `low + Math.random() * (high - low)`. Each run of a program produces a different sequence, and the sequence cannot be seeded. Each thread has its own sequence.

Do not use the result for passwords, tokens or anything else that must be unpredictable.

Nothing is borrowed or allocated.

console.name: log
console.documentation:
Writes formatted values to stdout, followed by a newline. Returns void; zero arguments print a blank line. Top-level strings print without quotes; arrays and records use structured inspection with quoted strings, a default depth of two and at most 100 array elements. Inputs are unchanged.

@param values - Zero or more int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, array or record values, evaluated once left to right. When the first value is a string and more arguments follow, %s substitutes text, %d a number, %i an integer prefix, %f a floating-point prefix, %j JSON, %o deeper inspection including array length, and %O default inspection. %c consumes a style argument; %% prints %. Missing substitutions remain literal; extra values are separated by spaces.

```tsrust
console.log("user: %s, age: %d", "Pat", 7); // stdout: user: Pat, age: 7
```

The compiler supports statically typed printable values, not functions, heterogeneous arrays, cyclic objects or custom inspectors. Native int retains its 64-bit range. Inputs remain available after logging.

Nullable values print their present payload, `null`, or `undefined`. For example, `const users = ["Alice"]; console.log(users.pop()); console.log(users.pop());` prints `Alice` then `undefined`. Inspection borrows owned payloads; logging does not consume them.

When the first value is a string and more arguments follow, %s substitutes text, %d a number, %i an integer prefix, %f a floating-point prefix, %j JSON, %o deeper inspection including array length, and %O default inspection. %c consumes a style argument; %% prints %. Missing substitutions remain literal; extra values are separated by spaces.

```tsrust
console.debug("user: %s, age: %d", "Pat", 7); // stdout: user: Pat, age: 7
```

The compiler supports statically typed printable values, not functions, heterogeneous arrays, cyclic objects or custom inspectors. Native int retains its 64-bit range. Inputs remain available after logging.

Nullable values print their present payload, `null`, or `undefined`. For example, `const users = ["Alice"]; console.log(users.pop()); console.log(users.pop());` prints `Alice` then `undefined`. Inspection borrows owned payloads; logging does not consume them.

assert
console.documentation:
Writes Assertion failed to stderr when condition is false-like; a string message follows after a colon, while non-string message values follow after a space. Does not throw or stop execution. Omitted condition is false-like; false, zero, NaN and empty text are false-like, while arrays and records are true-like.

@param condition - Optional printable value tested for truthiness.
@param values - Optional message using the same placeholders as log.

```tsrust
console.assert(false,"bad %d",7); // stderr: Assertion failed: bad 7
```

Returns void. Arguments evaluate once left to right; inputs are borrowed and remain unchanged. The supported values are native primitives, arrays and records. Functions, heterogeneous arrays and custom object inspectors are unsupported.

parameters: options?: {depth?: number, showHidden?: boolean, colors?: boolean}

console.documentation:
Alias of log: writes inspected values and format substitutions to stdout. No DOM tree visualization is available in this native terminal runtime.

@param values - Zero or more printable values; omission prints a blank line.

```tsrust
console.dirxml("value",7); // stdout: value 7
```

Returns void. Arguments evaluate once left to right; inputs are borrowed and remain unchanged. The supported values are native primitives, arrays and records. Functions, heterogeneous arrays and custom object inspectors are unsupported.

console.name: group
groupCollapsed
groupEnd
console.documentation:
Ends one console indentation level. Takes no arguments; unmatched calls leave indentation at zero. Writes nothing itself.

```tsrust
console.group();console.groupEnd();console.log(1); // stdout: 1
```

Returns void. Arguments evaluate once left to right; inputs are borrowed and remain unchanged. The supported values are native primitives, arrays and records. Functions, heterogeneous arrays and custom object inspectors are unsupported.

console.name: count
console.documentation:
Increments the counter identified by label and prints label: count to stdout, starting at 1.

@param label - Optional printable label converted to text; defaults to "default" when omitted or undefined. Records use [object Object]; arrays use comma-separated element text. Labels identify independent counters.

```tsrust
console.count("work");console.countReset("work"); // stdout: work: 1
```

Warnings are written immediately to stderr.

Returns void. Arguments evaluate once left to right; inputs are borrowed and remain unchanged. The supported values are native primitives, arrays and records. Functions, heterogeneous arrays and custom object inspectors are unsupported.

console.name: countReset
console.documentation:
Resets an existing named counter. Writes nothing on success; resetting a missing label writes a warning to stderr.

@param label - Optional string label; defaults to "default" when omitted or undefined. Non-string labels other than undefined warn and leave counters unchanged, even if count(label) created a counter using the converted text. Use the converted string explicitly to reset that counter, for example countReset("1") after count(1).

```tsrust
console.count("work");console.countReset("work"); // stdout: work: 1
```

Warnings are written immediately to stderr.

Returns void. Arguments evaluate once left to right; inputs are borrowed and remain unchanged. The supported values are native primitives, arrays and records. Functions, heterogeneous arrays and custom object inspectors are unsupported.

Reset labels are checked before conversion to text: explicit non-string labels (except default undefined) warn even if count created a matching text label. Pass the text label to reset it.

console.name: time
timeLog
timeEnd

Clears a terminal stdout screen and moves its cursor to the top-left. Takes no arguments. Does nothing when stdout is redirected or TERM is dumb; does not change group indentation. Uses ANSI terminal escape sequences.

```tsrust
console.clear(); // redirected stdout: no output
```

Returns void. Arguments evaluate once left to right; inputs are borrowed and remain unchanged. The supported values are native primitives, arrays and records. Functions, heterogeneous arrays and custom object inspectors are unsupported.

console.name: trace

@param values - Optional message with log-style placeholders.

```tsrust

```

Use this to identify the call path that reached a point in the program. Available frame names and source locations depend on debug symbols.
