boolean.name: valueOf
boolean.documentation:
Returns the same primitive value without conversion or boxing. Takes no arguments; the receiver is unchanged.

```tsrust
const value:boolean=true;console.log(value.valueOf()); // prints "true"
```

Primitive values are copied without allocation.

boolean.name: toString
boolean.documentation:
Returns "true" or "false" according to the receiver. Takes no arguments; the original boolean is unchanged.

```tsrust
const value:boolean=false;console.log(value.toString()); // prints "false"
```

Returns static borrowed text without allocating.

number.name: valueOf
number.documentation:
Returns the same primitive value without conversion or boxing. Takes no arguments; the receiver is unchanged.

```tsrust
const value:number=1.5;console.log(value.valueOf()); // prints "1.5"
```

Primitive values are copied without allocation.

number.name: toFixed
number.documentation:
Returns decimal text with fractionDigits places after the decimal point. Rounds halfway values to the nearest even digit (half to even). 0 through 100; omission means zero decimal places. Exact negative zero formats as positive zero. Special values use NaN and Infinity. JavaScript halfway rounding may differ.

@param fractionDigits - Integer number of digits after the decimal point, from 0 through 100; defaults to zero.

```tsrust
const value:number=1.25;console.log(value.toFixed(2)); // prints "1.25"
```

Receiver remains unchanged; result owns UTF-8 text. Precision must be int; invalid runtime bounds fail.

number.name: toExponential
number.documentation:
Returns scientific notation with fractionDigits places after the decimal point and a signed exponent. Rounds halfway values to the nearest even digit (half to even). 0 through 100; omission uses shortest scientific digits. Exact negative zero formats as positive zero. Special values use NaN and Infinity. JavaScript halfway rounding may differ.

@param fractionDigits - Integer number of digits after the decimal point, from 0 through 100; defaults to shortest scientific digits.

```tsrust
const value:number=1.25;console.log(value.toExponential(2)); // prints "1.25e+0"
```

Receiver remains unchanged; result owns UTF-8 text. Precision must be int; invalid runtime bounds fail.

number.name: toPrecision
number.documentation:
Returns text with precision significant digits, choosing decimal or scientific notation according to magnitude. Rounds halfway values to the nearest even digit (half to even). 1 through 100; omission uses shortest decimal digits. Exact negative zero formats as positive zero. Special values use NaN and Infinity. JavaScript halfway rounding may differ.

@param precision - Integer significant-digit count from 1 through 100; omission uses shortest decimal formatting.

```tsrust
const value:number=1.25;console.log(value.toPrecision(3)); // prints "1.25"
```

Receiver remains unchanged; result owns UTF-8 text. Precision must be int; invalid runtime bounds fail.

number.name: toString
number.documentation:
Returns the number as text. With no argument the text is the shortest decimal form that reads back as the same number. With a radix the number is written in that base.

@param radix - Optional int base from 2 through 36; digits above 9 are the lowercase letters `a` to `z`. Defaults to 10.

In another base, a fraction is written after a `.` using as many digits as are needed to read back the same number, so `0.1` in base 2 is a long repeating pattern. A negative number starts with `-`. `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` print as those words in every base, and negative zero prints as `0`. Very large or very small numbers use exponent form only in base 10, for example `1e+21`.

```tsrust
const value=255.5;console.log(value.toString(),value.toString(16),value.toString(2)); // prints "255.5 ff.8 11111111.1"
```

```tsrust
const third=1.0/3.0;console.log(third.toString(3),(0.1).toString(8),(-7.25).toString(2)); // prints "0.1 0.0631463146314631464 -111.01"
```

```tsrust
const big=1e21;console.log(big.toString(),big.toString(36),(0.0/0.0).toString(2)); // prints "1e+21 5v1j4f4ds7c000 NaN"
```

More than one argument is an `arity` error and a radix that is not an int is a `type` error. A radix outside 2 through 36 stops the program with `number.toString radix must be between 2 and 36` and the source position. Above 9007199254740992 a number cannot hold every whole value, so low digits it cannot represent print as `0`.

The receiver is copied; the result is a new string owned by the caller.

number.name: toLocaleString
number.documentation:
Formats a value as decimal text with a comma between each group of three integer digits. Takes no arguments. The decimal separator is a period; formatting is fixed and does not depend on the system language.

Fractional values round to at most three decimal places. Exactly halfway decimal values round away from zero. Trailing fractional zeros are removed. Even very large finite values use full decimal digits instead of exponent notation.

```tsrust
const value:number=1234.5675;const small:number=-0.0004;
console.log(value.toLocaleString(),small.toLocaleString()); // prints 1,234.568 -0
```

```tsrust
console.log(Number.NaN.toLocaleString(),Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY.toLocaleString(),Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY.toLocaleString());
// prints NaN ∞ -∞
```

Returns a new string and leaves the receiver unchanged. Negative zero retains its minus sign, including a negative value that rounds to zero. NaN gives `"NaN"`; infinities give `"∞"` and `"-∞"`. The number's shortest decimal text supplies the digits before decimal rounding.

Locale and options arguments are an `unsupported` error; remove them. Currency, alternate digits, grouping rules for other languages and custom precision are unavailable. These fixed display rules correspond to ordinary English decimal formatting.

Ownership: the numeric receiver is copied; the result owns its text.

int.name: valueOf
int.documentation:
Returns the same primitive value without conversion or boxing. Takes no arguments; the receiver is unchanged.

```tsrust
const value:int=7;console.log(value.valueOf()); // prints "7"
```

Primitive values are copied without allocation.

int.name: toString
int.documentation:
Formats a signed native i64 as lowercase digits. Optional radix is an int from 2 through 36, default 10. Negatives retain a leading minus in every radix; invalid radices fail.

@param radix - Integer base from 2 through 36, default 10; invalid bases fail.

```tsrust
const value:int=-255;console.log(value.toString(16)); // prints "-ff"
```

Supports the complete i64 range, unlike JavaScript Number’s safe-integer range. Receiver is copied; result owns independent UTF-8 text.

int.name: toLocaleString
int.documentation:
Formats a value as decimal text with a comma between each group of three integer digits. Takes no arguments. The decimal separator is a period; formatting is fixed and does not depend on the system language.

Formats the full signed 64-bit integer range exactly. There is no rounding or exponent notation.

```tsrust
const value:int=-1234567;console.log(value.toLocaleString(),value); // prints -1,234,567 -1234567
```

```tsrust
const value:int=9223372036854775807;console.log(value.toLocaleString());
// prints 9,223,372,036,854,775,807
```

Returns a new string and leaves the receiver unchanged. Zero gives `"0"`. Locale and options arguments are an `unsupported` error; remove them. Currency, alternate digits and grouping rules for other languages are unavailable. Integers outside the exact range of a floating-point number retain all their digits.

Ownership: the integer receiver is copied; the result owns its text.

globals.name: clone
globals.documentation:
Creates an independent copy of a cloneable owned value, preserving its type and active union variant. Accepts strings, arrays, records, Maps and unions with owned payloads, including Bytes and Result payloads. Owned descendants are copied recursively; static string text may remain safely shared. Null and undefined alternatives stay absent. Takes exactly one argument and returns the same type without mutating or consuming the source. Primitive scalars, Copy-only unions and ordinary callable environments are unsupported. Native types must explicitly permit independent cloning. Bytes clones have independent byte storage: later writes or resizing of either buffer cannot affect the other. This operation does not return Result; allocation failure is not guaranteed to be recoverable.

@param value - Required cloneable owned value, borrowed without consuming it. Preserves its type and active union variant.

```tsrust
import {alloc,at,set} from "std:bytes"; function main(){match(alloc(1,65)){Ok(bytes)=>{const other=clone(bytes);match(set(bytes,0,90)){Ok(_)=>{match(at(other,0)){Ok(value)=>{console.log(value);},Err(error)=>{console.log(error.message);}}},Err(error)=>{console.log(error.message);}}},Err(error)=>{console.log(error.message);}}}
```

Expected output: 65; writing 90 to the source leaves the clone unchanged.

Ownership: borrows the source and returns a new owner. Assignment and passing by value still transfer ownership without cloning.

globals.name: Result

examples.source: const result: Result<int, string> = Ok(5); match (result) { Ok(value) => { console.log(value); }, Err(_) => { console.log(-1); } }
const callback: Result<Function<int>, string> = Ok((): int => 7); match (callback) { Ok(action) => { console.log(action()); }, Err(_) => { console.log(-1); } }

function resultLength(result: ReadOnly<Result<string, int>>): int { match (result) { Ok(text) => { return text.length; }, Err(code) => { return code; } } } const borrowed: Result<string, int> = Ok("abc"); console.log(resultLength(borrowed), resultLength(borrowed));

function append(result: Mutable<Result<int[], string>>): void { match (result) { Ok(values) => { values.push(9); }, Err(_) => {} } } const editable: Result<int[], string> = Ok([1]); append(editable); append(editable); match (editable) { Ok(values) => { console.log(values.length); }, Err(_) => {} }

globals.name: Ok

examples.source: const result = Ok<int, string>(5); match (result) { Ok(value) => { console.log(value); }, Err(_) => { console.log(-1); } }

globals.name: Err

examples.source: const result = Err<int, string>("failed"); match (result) { Ok(_) => { console.log("unexpected"); }, Err(error) => { console.log(error); } }

globals.name: Number
globals.signature: Number(value?: int | number | boolean | string | null | undefined): number
parameters: value?: int | number | boolean | string | null | undefined
globals.documentation:
Converts scalar data to a number. Omission returns 0; null returns 0, undefined returns NaN, true returns 1 and false returns 0. Strings are trimmed using numeric whitespace and parsed as a whole decimal, signed Infinity or unsigned 0b/0o/0x integer; empty text returns 0 and invalid text returns NaN. Signed zero is preserved. A scalar union converts its active alternative without narrowing or changing the source. Use it to normalize numeric input before arithmetic.

@param value - Optional primitive scalar: int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined or scalar union. At most one argument; arrays, records and functions are type errors. Enums convert their underlying scalar value.

```tsrust
const value:string|undefined="12.5";console.log(Number(value),Number(true),Number(null),Number.isNaN(Number(undefined))); // 12.5 1 0 true
```

Returns a number using 64-bit floating-point precision; converting large int values may round. Radix prefixes accept either case, require at least one digit and cannot have a sign. Separators, BigInt suffixes and trailing text are invalid. BOM whitespace is accepted; U+0085 and U+200B are not whitespace. Unary + provides the same scalar conversion; an existing int expression keeps its int type under unary +. No boxed objects or custom valueOf conversion.

```tsrust
console.log(Number("0x10"),+"0b11",Number("0o17"),Number.isNaN(Number("12tail"))); // 16 3 15 true
```

Ownership: The argument is borrowed, remains reusable and evaluates once; the result is a copied scalar.

globals.name: null
globals.documentation:
Represents an explicitly empty value. Takes no arguments and has its own singleton type, distinct from undefined and void. Use null in variable/parameter/return annotations, record fields and homogeneous null[] arrays. Strict equality with null is also true for a JsonValue containing JSON null, including through optional unions; JSON null remains distinct from undefined. Comparisons borrow the JSON value and do not extract or consume it. Otherwise strict equality with null is true only for null; member access and arithmetic are rejected. Union annotations combine supported data alternatives with null and undefined, such as int|string|null. A strict null guard removes the null alternative at a stable named place. Optional fields follow their declared missing-value contract. Union array elements remain unsupported. Ownership: null itself has no owner to transfer; owned alternatives retain their ordinary ownership rules.

```tsrust
const value:null=null;console.log(value===null,typeof value,Number(value)); // true object 0
```

Matches JavaScript null semantics for supported operations, including typeof null returning object. This is a zero-sized copy value with no owned allocation.

globals.name: undefined
globals.documentation:
The read-only global missing-value constant. Takes no arguments. Distinct from null and from void, the unusable result type of a procedure. Supports annotations, parameters, returns, record fields and homogeneous undefined[] arrays. Local bindings/parameters may shadow the global; using a lexical binding before declaration is rejected. Union types and optional/defaulted parameters can include undefined. For example, int|string|undefined may hold any declared alternative. A strict undefined guard removes the missing alternative at a stable named place. Union array elements remain unsupported.

```tsrust
const missing:undefined=undefined;console.log(missing,Number(missing)); // undefined NaN
```

Console JSON placeholders omit undefined record fields and encode undefined array elements as null; logging prints undefined. A zero-sized copy value with no owned allocation.

globals.name: typeof
globals.documentation:
Returns the JavaScript type name as text. This is a unary operator, not a function. JsonValue reports the category of its contained JSON data: string, number, boolean or object. JSON null, arrays and objects all report object. The wrapper remains a JsonValue in storage. A stable boolean guard permits copying its boolean payload, including from JsonView or optional JSON values. A stable string guard enables length, startsWith, endsWith, includes, indexOf and lastIndexOf as borrowed text reads. A local inferred from a guarded JSON string is a StringView and may be returned while its source owner stays alive. String(view) explicitly copies to an owned string; assigning directly to string does not copy. A number guard preserves JsonValue storage. Use checked asInt or asNumber before arithmetic; asNumber rejects precision loss. No integer is implicitly rounded. number/int produce number; strings string; booleans boolean; undefined and void call results undefined; null, records and arrays object; callables function. A bare undeclared identifier produces undefined, while lexical use before declaration and unknown member/call expressions still fail. Namespace console/Math report object; Number and clone report function.

@param value - Expression evaluated once; its value is not consumed.

```tsrust
console.log(typeof null,typeof undefined,typeof [1],typeof absent); // object undefined object undefined
```

A union reports the category of its active alternative. Strict comparisons such as typeof value === "string", "number" === typeof value, or typeof value !== "boolean" narrow stable named bindings and record fields in the corresponding branches. Negation, logical guards and loop conditions retain the same stable-place rules. Replacing or mutating the place invalidates its proof. A computed array position is not a stable guard place; bind its value first. The "object" category includes null, arrays, tuples and all records, so this guard cannot distinguish them from one another.

Data unions may combine int, number, boolean, string, records, arrays, tuples, null and undefined. Member order and duplicate alternatives do not change identity. Callable unions still require one callable payload with optional null/undefined. Access members only after proving the required alternative. An optional member operation requires one proven present type; common methods across different alternatives are not inferred. A union value compares with `===` and `!==` against an int, number, boolean or string, or against another union of such values; values with different alternatives are unequal, except that int and number compare by value. Where the comparison with one value is true, the union variable is narrowed to that value's type, so `if (value === "yes") { value.toUpperCase(); }` is accepted. Arithmetic on a union and ambiguous inference across several unresolved generic patterns remain unsupported; narrow first. Supply explicit type arguments when inference is ambiguous.

```tsrust
const value:int|string|boolean="text";
if(typeof value==="string"){console.log(value.toUpperCase());} // prints "TEXT"
```

Native int and number both report "number"; this does not change int arithmetic or distinguish these alternatives. Use Number(value) when a numeric union needs a common numeric result. Non-null assertions remove only null and undefined and preserve every other alternative. The argument remains unchanged and the result is static text.

Ownership: Owned union alternatives retain their owners. typeof and readonly observations borrow them; clone() copies supported owning data independently. Mutable data parameters borrow supplied owners, including staged spread arguments. Defaulted parameters use fresh local default owners when omitted.

```tsrust
function main(){const value=JSON.parse('"hello"');console.log(typeof value,typeof JSON.parse("null"));const flag=JSON.parse('true');if(typeof flag==='boolean'){const result:boolean=flag;console.log(result);}const text=JSON.parse('"hello"');if(typeof text==='string'){const borrowed=text;console.log(borrowed.length,borrowed.includes('ell'));}}
```

Expected output: string object, then true, then 5 true on separate lines. The JSON value is borrowed and remains usable.

examples.source: function main(){const value=JSON.parse('"hello"');console.log(typeof value,typeof JSON.parse("null"));const flag=JSON.parse('true');if(typeof flag==='boolean'){const result:boolean=flag;console.log(result);}const text=JSON.parse('"hello"');if(typeof text==='string'){const borrowed=text;console.log(borrowed.length,borrowed.includes('ell'));}}

globals.name: void
globals.documentation:
Evaluates an expression exactly once, discards its result and returns undefined. This unary operator differs from the void procedure return annotation: a void call alone cannot be stored, but void call() produces a usable undefined value. It does not throw away type errors or skip effects.

@param expression - Expression evaluated for its effects; owned named inputs are borrowed, not moved.

```tsrust
let count=0;const missing:undefined=void count++;console.log(count,missing); // 1 undefined
```

Does not enable dynamic coercion. The void result type cannot be a union member; the value undefined can. Temporary results are disposed after evaluation; the result is a zero-sized copy value.

globals.name: Boolean
globals.documentation:
Converts a supported value to primitive truthiness. Returns false for omission, null, undefined, a void call result, false, zero (including -0), NaN and empty text. Every nonempty string, array, record and callable is true; empty arrays/records are true too. For a nullable union, tests the active payload, null or undefined variant using the same truthiness rules. Does not mutate inputs or construct a boxed Boolean object. Additional arguments evaluate left to right but are ignored.

@param value - Optional primitive, array, record or callable; defaults to undefined.

```tsrust
console.log(Boolean(null),Boolean("false"),Boolean([])); // false true true
```

new Boolean and arbitrary dynamic/host objects are not supported. Native conditions still require boolean; use this explicit conversion rather than assuming general implicit coercion. Whole unions are borrowed without unwrapping or narrowing their declared type. Named inputs are borrowed; the boolean result has no owned allocation.

globals.name: String
globals.documentation:
Converts a supported value to primitive text. Omission returns empty text, explicit null returns null and undefined/void call results return undefined. Booleans use true/false, numbers use decimal/exponent text (NaN/Infinity supported; -0 becomes 0). Arrays join element text with commas; null/undefined slots become empty text and nested arrays flatten their textual joins. Fixed typed tuples use the same array text rules. Records return [object Object]. A data union converts its active alternative using these rules, or produces null/undefined text for those variants. Does not mutate inputs or construct boxed String objects. Additional arguments evaluate once left to right but are ignored.

@param value - Optional primitive, array or record; no argument differs from explicit undefined. Callable source-text conversion is rejected, including whole nullable unions with a callable payload even when currently null or undefined. First use a strict guard to narrow the argument to a supported null, undefined or data alternative.

```tsrust
console.log(String(null),String(undefined),String([null,null]),String(-0.0)); // null undefined , 0
```

No custom toString/valueOf, Symbol conversion or dynamic host objects. Native int retains its signed 64-bit domain. Whole data unions are observed without unwrapping or narrowing their declared type. Named inputs are borrowed and remain reusable; owned string inputs produce an independent copy. Arrays are read directly into one independently owned result string, including all supported nested-array text. Additional arguments still evaluate left to right while the source remains protected.

globals.name: Array
globals.documentation:
Provides supported static array functions. Array.isArray tests whether a value is an array and returns a boolean; this differs from instance methods such as values.map or values.includes. Array.of constructs a typed dense array. Array.from creates an independent array from an array, Unicode string characters, Set values or Map key/value tuples, optionally mapping each item and its index. The general Array constructor is unavailable. Array literals support ordered spreads: `[0, ...values, 1]` appends every source element in order. Each segment evaluates once from left to right; spreading copies scalar elements and transfers owned elements. Strings, Sets and Maps can also supply elements. Declared union elements retain compatible alternatives. Arbitrary iterator objects and sparse slots are unsupported.

```tsrust
console.log(Array.isArray([1]),Array.isArray(null)); // true false
```

Only statically typed native values are represented; arbitrary JavaScript proxies/host objects are unsupported. Static checks borrow their operands without transferring ownership.

Array.of and array literals accept spread sources from arrays, strings, Sets and Maps. Scalar elements copy; owned collection elements and Map tuples transfer. Strings construct Unicode scalar character values.

globals.name: Function
globals.documentation:
The type of a function value: a named function, an arrow function, or a callable stored in a variable, field or array.

`Result` is the type the function returns; use `void` when it returns nothing. `[Arguments]` is an optional list of argument types in call order. Leaving it out means the function takes no arguments, so `Function<int>` is called as `action()`. An argument can have a label (`text: string`), be optional (`limit?: int`), or collect the remaining values (`...rest: int[]`). Labels do not change the type; they appear in parameter help. A required argument cannot follow an optional one, and a rest argument must be last.

```tsrust
const double: Function<int, [int]> = (value: int): int => { return value * 2; };
console.log(double(4)); // prints "8"
```

```tsrust
const pick: Function<int, [first: int, second?: int, ...rest: int[]]> = (first: int, second?: int, ...rest: int[]): int => { return first + rest.length; };
console.log(pick(1), pick(1, 2, 3, 4)); // prints "1 3"
```

An argument that owns data (a string, array or record) must say how the function uses it: `ReadOnly<T>`, `Mutable<T>` or `Owned<T>`. `Function<int, [string]>` is a `callback-access` error; write `Function<int, [ReadOnly<string>]>`. Scalars such as `int` are copied and take no wrapper. `Function` with no result type is a `type` error, and arguments not written as a list, such as `Function<int, string>`, are a `syntax` error.

This is an exact signature, not the loose JavaScript `Function` type: argument count and types are checked at every call.

Ownership: a plain `Function<...>` owns its captured values. Passing or assigning it transfers the function, and it can be called many times. Wrap it in `ReadOnly`, `Mutable` or `Once` to borrow it or to make it single-use.

examples.source:
const double: Function<int, [int]> = (value: int): int => { return value * 2; };
console.log(double(4));

const pick: Function<int, [first: int, second?: int, ...rest: int[]]> = (first: int, second?: int, ...rest: int[]): int => { return first + rest.length; };
console.log(pick(1), pick(1, 2, 3, 4));

globals.name: Mutable
globals.documentation:
Lends something for the duration of a call and allows it to be changed.

`T` is one type. Around a function type, `Mutable<Function<...>>` borrows a callback that may change the values it captured; the caller keeps the callback and can pass it again afterwards. Around an argument inside a `Function` argument list, `Mutable<T>` means the function changes the caller's string, array or record in place.

```tsrust
let calls = 0;
const count: Mutable<Function<int>> = (): int => { calls += 1; return calls; };
console.log(count(), count()); // prints "1 2"
```

```tsrust
const values = [1];
const grow: ReadOnly<Function<int, [Mutable<int[]>]>> = (list: int[]): int => { list.push(2); return list.length; };
console.log(grow(values), values.join(",")); // prints "2 1,2"
```

A borrowed callback cannot be returned, stored in a record or array, or captured by a returned function; that is a `callback-escape` error. Passing the same value as two `Mutable` arguments of one call is a `conflicting-access` error. `Mutable` around a scalar such as `int`, or around a data type outside a `Function` argument list, is a `callback-access` error. Wrappers do not nest: `ReadOnly<Mutable<T>>` is rejected.

Ownership: nothing is copied or moved. The caller remains the owner, and the loan ends when the call returns.

globals.name: ReadOnly
globals.documentation:
Lends something for the duration of a call without allowing it to be changed.

`T` is one type. Around a function type, `ReadOnly<Function<...>>` borrows a callback that only reads the values it captured; it can be called any number of times and the caller keeps it. Around an argument inside a `Function` argument list, `ReadOnly<T>` means the function reads the caller's string, array or record and leaves it unchanged.

```tsrust
const text = "abc";
const size: ReadOnly<Function<int>> = (): int => { return text.length; };
console.log(size(), size(), text); // prints "3 3 abc"
```

```tsrust
const measure: ReadOnly<Function<int, [ReadOnly<string>]>> = (text: string): int => { return text.length; };
const word = "four";
console.log(measure(word), word); // prints "4 four"
```

A callback that changes or consumes a captured value does not fit `ReadOnly<Function<...>>` and is a `callback-access` error. A borrowed callback cannot be returned or stored (`callback-escape`). `ReadOnly` around a scalar such as `int`, or around a data type outside a `Function` argument list, is a `callback-access` error.

This describes borrowing for one call. It is not TypeScript's `Readonly<T>`, which makes object properties read-only.

Ownership: nothing is copied or moved. The caller remains the owner and can keep using the value after the call.

globals.name: Once
globals.documentation:
A function value that can be called exactly one time.

`T` must be a function type, as in `Once<Function<string>>`. The single call may move the values the function captured out of it, for example returning a captured string without copying it.

```tsrust
const label = "done".repeat(1);
const finish: Once<Function<string>> = (): string => { return label; };
console.log(finish()); // prints "done"
```

Calling the same `Once` function a second time is a `closure-consumed` error for a local value and a `callback-consumed` error for a parameter. `Once` around anything other than a function type, such as `Once<int>`, is a `callback-access` error; use `Owned<T>` for a data argument.

Ownership: the function is owned. Passing it transfers it, and calling it uses it up.

globals.name: Owned
globals.documentation:
Marks an argument that the function takes over, or spells out that a function value is owned.

`T` is one type. Around an argument inside a `Function` argument list, `Owned<T>` means the caller gives the string, array or record to the function; the function can keep it, return it or let it go. Around a function type, `Owned<Function<...>>` means the same as plain `Function<...>`.

```tsrust
const keep: ReadOnly<Function<string, [Owned<string>]>> = (text: string): string => { return text; };
console.log(keep("moved".repeat(1))); // prints "moved"
```

After a value is passed as an `Owned` argument the caller can no longer use it; a later use is a `transferred` error. Pass `clone(value)` to keep the original. `Owned` around a scalar such as `int`, or around a data type outside a `Function` argument list, is a `callback-access` error.

Ownership: the value moves into the function without copying.

examples.source:
const keep: ReadOnly<Function<string, [Owned<string>]>> = (text: string): string => { return text; };
console.log(keep("moved".repeat(1)));

globals.name: Object
globals.documentation:
Provides functions that work on any value. `Object.is` tests whether two values are the same value, treating `NaN` as itself and telling `0` from `-0`.

```tsrust
console.log(Object.is(1,1),Object.is("a","b")); // prints "true false"
```

Object is a namespace of functions here; it is not a constructor and cannot be called or used as a type.

globals.name: parseInt
globals.documentation:
Reads a whole number from the start of a string and returns it as a number. It is the same function as `Number.parseInt`. Leading spaces are skipped, an optional `+` or `-` sign is accepted, and reading stops at the first character that is not a digit of the radix, so trailing text is ignored.

@param text - String to read. It is not changed.
@param radix - Optional int base from 2 through 36; letters `a` to `z` (either case) are digits above 9. When omitted or `0`, base 10 is used, or base 16 when the digits start with `0x` or `0X`.

@returns A `number`. `NaN` when no digit can be read, for example an empty string or `"abc"`, and when the radix is outside 2 through 36. A fraction is not read: `"3.9"` gives `3`.

```tsrust
console.log(parseInt("42px"), parseInt("  -17"), parseInt("3.9")); // prints "42 -17 3"
```

```tsrust
console.log(parseInt("ff", 16), parseInt("0x1F"), parseInt("101", 2), parseInt("abc")); // prints "255 31 5 NaN"
```

Calling it with no argument or more than two is an `arity` error. The text must be a string and the radix an int, otherwise a `type` error. The result is a `number`, not an `int`, because it can be `NaN`; assigning it to an `int` is a `type` error. Passing `parseInt` itself as a value, as in `texts.map(parseInt)`, is unsupported; write `texts.map((text) => parseInt(text))`. A function or variable that you declare with the name `parseInt` takes precedence.

The string is borrowed for the call and stays usable; the result is a plain number.

globals.name: parseFloat
globals.documentation:
Reads a decimal number from the start of a string and returns it as a number. It is the same function as `Number.parseFloat`. Leading spaces are skipped. An optional sign, digits, a fraction, an exponent and the word `Infinity` are accepted, and reading stops at the first character that does not continue the number.

@param text - String to read. It is not changed.

@returns A `number`. `NaN` when the text does not start with a number, for example an empty string or `"abc"`.

```tsrust
console.log(parseFloat("1.25tail"), parseFloat("  -2e3"), parseFloat(".5"), parseFloat("abc")); // prints "1.25 -2000 0.5 NaN"
```

Exactly one string argument is required: another count is an `arity` error and another type a `type` error. A value too large for a number gives `Infinity`. Passing `parseFloat` itself as a value is unsupported; wrap it in an arrow function. A function or variable that you declare with the name `parseFloat` takes precedence.

The string is borrowed for the call and stays usable; the result is a plain number.

globals.name: isNaN
globals.documentation:
Tests whether a number is `NaN`, the result of an undefined numeric operation such as `0.0 / 0.0` or of reading a number from text that has none. It is the same function as `Number.isNaN`.

@param value - Number to test. An int is accepted and is never `NaN`.

@returns `true` only for `NaN`; `false` for every other number, including the infinities.

```tsrust
const parsed = parseInt("abc"); console.log(isNaN(parsed), isNaN(1.5), isNaN(Infinity), parsed === NaN); // prints "true false false false"
```

Use this function instead of `value === NaN`, which is always `false`. Exactly one number is required: another count is an `arity` error, and a string, boolean or other type is a `type` error because no value is converted to a number first; convert explicitly with `Number(value)`. A function or variable that you declare with the name `isNaN` takes precedence.

The number is copied; nothing is changed or allocated.

examples.source: const parsed = parseInt("abc"); console.log(isNaN(parsed), isNaN(1.5), isNaN(Infinity), parsed === NaN);

globals.name: isFinite
globals.documentation:
Tests whether a number is an ordinary finite value. It is the same function as `Number.isFinite`.

@param value - Number to test. An int is accepted and is always finite.

@returns `false` for `Infinity`, `-Infinity` and `NaN`; `true` for every other number.

```tsrust
console.log(isFinite(2.5), isFinite(1.0 / 0.0), isFinite(-Infinity), isFinite(NaN)); // prints "true false false false"
```

Exactly one number is required: another count is an `arity` error, and a string, boolean or other type is a `type` error because no value is converted to a number first; convert explicitly with `Number(value)`. A function or variable that you declare with the name `isFinite` takes precedence.

The number is copied; nothing is changed or allocated.

globals.name: NaN
globals.documentation:
The not-a-number value, the same value as `Number.NaN`. Arithmetic produces it for an undefined result such as `0.0 / 0.0`, and `parseInt` and `parseFloat` return it when text holds no number. It takes no arguments.

```tsrust
const missing = NaN; console.log(missing, missing === NaN, isNaN(missing), missing + 1.0, typeof missing); // prints "NaN false true NaN number"
```

`NaN` is not equal to any value, itself included, so `value === NaN` is always `false`; test with `isNaN(value)`. Any arithmetic with `NaN` gives `NaN`, and every ordering comparison with it is `false`. Its type is `number`; assigning it to an `int` is a `type` error. It cannot be assigned to. A variable or parameter that you declare with the name `NaN` takes precedence.

The value is a plain copied number.

examples.source: const missing = NaN; console.log(missing, missing === NaN, isNaN(missing), missing + 1.0, typeof missing);

globals.name: Infinity
globals.documentation:
The positive infinite number, the same value as `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`. It is greater than every other number. Write `-Infinity` for the negative infinite number. It takes no arguments.

```tsrust
let lowest = Infinity; for (const value of [4.5, 2.5, 8.0]) { if (value < lowest) { lowest = value; } } console.log(lowest, Infinity > Number.MAX_VALUE, -Infinity, isFinite(Infinity)); // prints "2.5 true -Infinity false"
```

A common use is the starting value of a running minimum (`Infinity`) or maximum (`-Infinity`). `isFinite(Infinity)` is `false`. `Infinity - Infinity` and `Infinity * 0.0` give `NaN`. Its type is `number`; assigning it to an `int` is a `type` error. It cannot be assigned to. A variable or parameter that you declare with the name `Infinity` takes precedence.

The value is a plain copied number.

examples.source: let lowest = Infinity; for (const value of [4.5, 2.5, 8.0]) { if (value < lowest) { lowest = value; } } console.log(lowest, Infinity > Number.MAX_VALUE, -Infinity, isFinite(Infinity));

globals.name: Set
globals.signature: new Set<Element>(source?: Element[] | Set<Element> | string | null | undefined): Set<Element>
parameters: source?: Element[] | Set<Element> | string | null | undefined
globals.documentation:
Constructs an owned set of unique keys in insertion order. Without a source, use an explicit key type or a contextual Set type. Arrays and sets provide keys; strings provide Unicode characters and require string keys. Null and undefined create an empty set. Duplicate keys are omitted; negative number zero is stored as positive zero. Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]);
console.log(values.size); // 2
```

Ownership: construction explicitly copies source keys; the source remains usable. Ordinary bindings and access never implicitly clone a set.

globals.name: Map
globals.signature: new Map<Key, Value>(source?: [Key, Value][] | Map<Key, Value> | null | undefined): Map<Key, Value>
parameters: source?: [Key, Value][] | Map<Key, Value> | null | undefined
globals.documentation:
Constructs an owned map of keys and values in insertion order. With no source, use explicit key/value types or a contextual Map type. Entry arrays contain exactly two-element key/value tuples; another Map supplies its entries. Null and undefined create an empty map. Repeated keys replace the value and keep their first insertion position. Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>();
values.set("a", 1);
console.log(values.size); // 1
```

Ownership: construction explicitly copies source keys and values; the source remains usable. Values that cannot be cloned cannot be copied through a source constructor. Access and ordinary bindings never implicitly clone a Map.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.size);

ArrayConstructor.name: isArray
ArrayConstructor.documentation:
Tests whether a supported value is an array. JsonValue is inspected by its contained data: JSON arrays return true; all other JSON kinds return false. Returns true for any native homogeneous array, including empty/nested arrays and fixed typed tuple values; false for scalars, null, undefined, records, callables and void call results. For a data union, inspects its active alternative: an array or fixed tuple is true and any other alternative is false. Omission returns false. The operand is evaluated once; additional arguments evaluate left to right and are ignored. Inputs are unchanged.

@param value - Optional value to classify; defaults to undefined.

```tsrust
console.log(Array.isArray([]),Array.isArray({a:1}),Array.isArray(undefined)); // true false false
```

Does not implement proxies, boxed values, dynamic heterogeneous arrays or the Array constructor. This observation by itself does not narrow a union or permit member/index projection. Strict null/undefined guards can prove a payload at a stable named place; replacing or consuming it invalidates that proof. The boolean result does not allocate; owned operands are borrowed for the call.

```tsrust
function main(){const value=JSON.parse("[null]");console.log(Array.isArray(value),value===null,JSON.parse("null")===null);}
```

Expected output: true false true. JSON arrays may contain mixed JSON kinds; inspection does not grant unchecked element access.

std:os.name: endianness
std:os.documentation:
Returns the CPU byte order for which the executable was compiled: BE for big endian or LE for little endian. Takes no arguments and has no defaults. The result is constant during execution, including execution under translation. It follows the executable compilation target, not physical hardware. An unsupported byte-order selector produces a native compilation error. No receiver or external state is mutated.

```tsrust
import { endianness } from "std:os";
function main() { const order = endianness(); console.log(order === "BE" || order === "LE"); } // true
```

Ownership: returns an independent string value.

examples.source:
import { endianness } from "std:os";
function main() { const order = endianness(); console.log(order === "BE" || order === "LE"); }

std:os.name: platform

examples.source:
import { platform } from 'std:os';
function main() { console.log(platform() === platform()); }

std:os.documentation:
Returns the executable compilation target’s operating-system name. Takes no arguments and has no defaults. Returns one of aix, android, darwin, freebsd, linux, openbsd, sunos or win32; the result remains constant during execution. It describes the compiled executable, including a translated executable, rather than physical hardware. Unsupported target components produce a native compilation error. No receiver or external state is mutated.

```tsrust
import { platform } from 'std:os';
function main() { console.log(platform() === platform()); } // prints true
```

Ownership: returns an independent string value.

std:os.name: arch

examples.source:
import { arch } from 'std:os';
function main() { console.log(arch() === arch()); }

std:os.documentation:
Returns the executable compilation target’s CPU architecture name. Takes no arguments and has no defaults. Returns one of arm, arm64, ia32, loong64, mips, mipsel, ppc64, riscv64, s390x or x64; the result remains constant during execution. It describes the compiled executable, including a translated executable, rather than physical hardware. Unsupported target components produce a native compilation error. No receiver or external state is mutated.

```tsrust
import { arch } from 'std:os';
function main() { console.log(arch() === arch()); } // prints true
```

Ownership: returns an independent string value.

std:path.name: join

parameters.name: paths
parameters.label: ...paths: string[]
parameters.documentation: Zero or more ordinary string segments in order. Empty segments are ignored. Each segment is borrowed; non-string scalars or spread elements are rejected.

std:path.documentation:
Composes zero or more string path segments and normalizes the result lexically. Pass ordinary string arguments or spread a homogeneous string array. Empty segments are ignored; no segments or only empty segments return a dot. Joins with a slash on POSIX and a backslash on Windows. Later rooted segments do not replace earlier segments. Dot and parent segments collapse; trailing separators can remain. Windows drive-relative paths retain their drive prefix. UNC intent is preserved when the first nonempty segment starts with exactly two separators followed by a non-separator; otherwise repeated leading Windows separators collapse to one before normalization. Reserved device names followed by a colon in a backslash-delimited component can retain dot and parent segments while forward slashes become backslashes. No filesystem access, symlink resolution or containment guarantee is provided. Non-string arguments are compile-time errors. There are no optional defaults, receiver mutations or public argument-count limit.

```tsrust
import { join } from "std:path";
function main() { console.log(join("reports", "..", "archive")); console.log(join()); } // prints archive, then .
```

Ownership: direct calls and known native stored/aliased calls borrow segments and spread arrays; the result owns its text. Passing the value through an abstract Function rest contract transfers its tail values according to that contract, without implicit string clones.

examples.source:
import { join } from "std:path";
function main() { console.log(join("reports", "..", "archive")); console.log(join()); }

std:path.name: basename

parameters.label: path: string
parameters.documentation: The path text to examine. No file needs to exist.

parameters.label: suffix?: string
parameters.documentation: An optional, case-sensitive ending to remove. Omitted or empty leaves the last component unchanged.

examples.source: import { basename } from 'std:path';function apply(action:Mutable<Function<string, [path:ReadOnly<string>]>>):string{return action('/tmp/report.txt');}function main(){const f=basename;console.log(f('/tmp/report.txt'));console.log(f('/tmp/report.txt','.txt'));console.log(apply(basename));console.log(apply(f));console.log(f('/tmp/report.txt','.txt'));}

import { basename } from 'std:path';function factory():(path:ReadOnly<string>)=>string{const selected=basename;return selected;}function main(){const f=factory();console.log(f('/tmp/report.txt'));console.log(f('/tmp/other.txt'));}

import { basename } from 'std:path';function identity(action:Once<Function<string, [path:ReadOnly<string>]>>):(path:ReadOnly<string>)=>string{return action;}function main(){const f=basename;const next=identity(f);console.log(next('/tmp/report.txt'));}

import { basename as first,basename as second } from 'std:path';function main(){const selected=first;console.log((true?selected:second)('/tmp/report.txt'));console.log((false?first:second)('/tmp/report.txt','.txt'));}

Object.name: is
Object.documentation:
Tests whether two values are the same value. It is stricter about numbers than `===`: `NaN` is the same as `NaN`, and `0` is not the same as `-0`.

@param left - First value.
@param right - Second value. Both are evaluated once, left then right, and neither is changed.

Returns a boolean. Numbers are the same when they have the same value; an `int` and a `number` with the same value are the same. Strings are the same when their text is equal. Booleans, `null` and `undefined` are the same as themselves. Values of different kinds are never the same.

```tsrust
console.log(Object.is(Number.NaN,Number.NaN),Object.is(0.0,-0.0),Object.is(1,1.0)); // prints "true false true"
```

```tsrust
const a=[1];const b=[1];console.log(Object.is(a,a),Object.is(a,b),Object.is("x","x")); // prints "true false true"
```

```tsrust
console.log(Object.is(1,"1"),Object.is(null,undefined),Object.is(null,null)); // prints "false false true"
```

An array or record is the same only as itself: two separate arrays with equal contents are not the same, and neither are two array literals. Calling it with fewer or more than two arguments is an `arity` error. Functions and unions containing callable values are not accepted and give an `unsupported` error. Data unions such as `string | null` are supported.

Both values are borrowed for the comparison and stay usable.

Data unions compare their active alternatives using the same rules. Null and undefined compare only with themselves. Numeric payloads retain NaN and signed-zero rules; array and record payloads compare storage identity without cloning.

Object.name: keys
Object.documentation:
Returns the own enumerable property names of a supported value as a new string array.

@param value - One record, tuple, array, string, int, number or boolean. Records return their declared field names in the order of that value's constructor literal, even when that order differs from its type declaration. Field replacement and clone() preserve this order. Arrays and tuples return decimal position names from "0" through length minus one. Strings return decimal UTF-16 code-unit positions, so a supplementary character contributes two names. Numbers and booleans return an empty array.

The value is evaluated once and remains unchanged. The result is independent and may be changed or iterated with for...of. Empty arrays return an empty result. Exactly one argument is required; missing or extra arguments are an arity error. Null, undefined, nullable values and functions are unsupported. Records have fixed fields; dynamic additions, deletions, prototype properties and symbol keys are unavailable. Numeric and quoted record property declarations are unsupported.

```tsrust
type Row={first:int;second:string;};
const row:Row={second:"x",first:1};
console.log(Object.keys(row).join(",")); // prints "second,first"
```

```tsrust
console.log(Object.keys("é😀").join(","),Object.keys(true).length); // prints "0,1,2 0"
```

Ownership: The argument is borrowed. The returned array owns its entries independently of the argument.

type EntriesRow = { id: int; name: string; }; const row: EntriesRow = { name: "ada", id: 7 };
for (const pair of Object.entries(row)) { console.log(pair[0], String(pair[1])); }

type EntriesSize = { w: int; h: int; }; const size: EntriesSize = { w: 4, h: 5 };

Set.name: size
Set.documentation:
Returns the number of distinct keys. Readonly; assigning this property is rejected.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); console.log(values.size); // 2
```

Set.name: add
Set.documentation:
Inserts a key if absent. A duplicate leaves order unchanged. Returns void; chaining is unsupported. Deleting and adding a key again places it last. Ownership: owned keys transfer into the set; scalar keys copy.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); values.add(3); console.log(values.size); // 3
```

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); values.add(3); console.log(values.size);

Set.name: has
Set.documentation:
Reports whether a matching key exists. Receiver and argument are borrowed and unchanged.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); console.log(values.has(2)); // true
```

Set.name: delete
Set.documentation:
Removes a matching key and returns true, or returns false if absent. Surviving keys keep their order. Argument is borrowed; receiver mutates.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); console.log(values.delete(2), values.size); // true 1
```

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); console.log(values.delete(2), values.size);

Set.name: clear
Set.documentation:
Removes every key. Returns void. Receiver mutates.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); values.clear(); console.log(values.size); // 0
```

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); values.clear(); console.log(values.size);

Set.name: values
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent array of keys in insertion order. Takes no arguments. This is an array snapshot, not a live iterator. Receiver is borrowed; keys are explicitly copied.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); console.log(values.values().join(",")); // 2,1
```

Set.name: keys
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent array of keys in insertion order, like values(). Takes no arguments. Receiver is borrowed; keys are explicitly copied.

Keys are int, number, boolean, string, null, undefined, enums, or unions of those values. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN and both zeros are the same key. Record, array, and function identity keys are unsupported.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([2, 1, 2]); console.log(values.keys().join(",")); // 2,1
```

Set.name: entries
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent array of key/key tuples in insertion order. Takes no arguments and does not mutate the receiver. Each tuple contains the same key in both positions. An empty Set returns an empty array. Replacement does not change order; deletion and reinsertion places a key last. Number keys use SameValueZero, including NaN and normalized zero. Wrong argument counts are static errors. This operation returns an array snapshot rather than a live iterator.

Example: `const values = new Set<string>(["b", "a", "b"]); const pairs = values.entries(); console.log(pairs[0][0], pairs[0][1]);` prints `b b`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<string>(["b", "a", "b"]); const pairs = values.entries(); console.log(pairs[0][0], pairs[0][1]);
// prints b b
```

Ownership: explicitly copies owned keys into both tuple positions. Later receiver mutation does not change the snapshot.

examples.source: const values = new Set<string>(["b", "a", "b"]); const pairs = values.entries(); console.log(pairs[0][0], pairs[0][1]);

Set.name: forEach
Set.signature: forEach(callback: (value: Element, key: Element, source: Set<Element>) => Result): void
parameters: callback: (value: Element, key: Element, source: Set<Element>) => Result
Set.documentation:
Calls a reusable callback once for each key in insertion order. The callback receives the value, the same key again, and the readonly source Set. Callbacks may use zero through three supplied positions; normal default and rest parameter rules apply. An empty Set does not call the callback. There is no thisArg argument. Wrong arity, incompatible parameter types/access, consuming callbacks, and receiver mutation or transfer during iteration are static errors.

Returns void and does not mutate the receiver. Callback results are evaluated and discarded after each call. Callback errors propagate and may be caught by surrounding try/catch. External mutable captures are allowed when they do not conflict with receiver borrows.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 3]); let total = 0; values.forEach((value) => { total = total + value; }); console.log(total);` prints `4`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 3]); let total = 0; values.forEach((value) => { total = total + value; }); console.log(total);
// prints 4
```

Ownership: scalar inputs copy; owned key arguments and the source Set borrow readonly. No owned callback input is implicitly cloned.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 3]); let total = 0; values.forEach((value) => { total = total + value; }); console.log(total);

Set.name: isSubsetOf
Set.documentation:
Tests whether every receiver key occurs in another Set. Takes exactly one other Set, whose key type may differ from the receiver. Returns a boolean and does not mutate either input. An empty receiver returns true. Wrong arity, a non-Set argument, and conflicting mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Keys follow existing native key equality: NaN equals NaN, negative zero equals zero, and compatible numeric alternatives can match. Distinct string/boolean/null/undefined alternatives do not match; enum keys retain their enum type identity. Large int-to-number comparisons can lose precision.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([1, 2]); console.log(values.isSubsetOf(new Set<int>([1, 2, 3])));` prints `true`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([1, 2]); console.log(values.isSubsetOf(new Set<int>([1, 2, 3])));
// prints true
```

Ownership: both Sets and their owned keys borrow readonly. No keys are cloned or transferred.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([1, 2]); console.log(values.isSubsetOf(new Set<int>([1, 2, 3])));

Set.name: isSupersetOf
Set.documentation:
Tests whether every key in another Set occurs in the receiver. Takes exactly one other Set, whose key type may differ from the receiver. Returns a boolean and does not mutate either input. An empty argument returns true. Wrong arity, a non-Set argument, and conflicting mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Keys follow existing native key equality: NaN equals NaN, negative zero equals zero, and compatible numeric alternatives can match. Distinct string/boolean/null/undefined alternatives do not match; enum keys retain their enum type identity. Large int-to-number comparisons can lose precision.

Example: `const values = new Set<string>(["a", "b"]); console.log(values.isSupersetOf(new Set<string>(["b"])));` prints `true`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<string>(["a", "b"]); console.log(values.isSupersetOf(new Set<string>(["b"])));
// prints true
```

Ownership: both Sets and their owned keys borrow readonly. No keys are cloned or transferred.

examples.source: const values = new Set<string>(["a", "b"]); console.log(values.isSupersetOf(new Set<string>(["b"])));

Set.name: isDisjointFrom
Set.documentation:
Tests whether the receiver and another Set share no keys. Takes exactly one other Set, whose key type may differ from the receiver. Returns a boolean and does not mutate either input. If either Set is empty, returns true. Wrong arity, a non-Set argument, and conflicting mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Keys follow existing native key equality: NaN equals NaN, negative zero equals zero, and compatible numeric alternatives can match. Distinct string/boolean/null/undefined alternatives do not match; enum keys retain their enum type identity. Large int-to-number comparisons can lose precision.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([1, 2]); console.log(values.isDisjointFrom(new Set<string>(["1", "2"])));` prints `true`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([1, 2]); console.log(values.isDisjointFrom(new Set<string>(["1", "2"])));
// prints true
```

Ownership: both Sets and their owned keys borrow readonly. No keys are cloned or transferred.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([1, 2]); console.log(values.isDisjointFrom(new Set<string>(["1", "2"])));

Set.name: union
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent Set containing keys from either input. Takes exactly one Set; its key type may differ. Neither input is mutated. Receiver keys come first, followed by new keys in other insertion order. Empty inputs follow these same rules. Wrong arity, non-Set arguments and conflicting receiver mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Key comparisons retain existing native SameValueZero and enum identity rules. Large int/number overlap can lose precision. Union and symmetric difference infer a joined key type; intersection and difference keep the receiver key type.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([3, 1]); const result = values.union(new Set<int>([1, 2])); console.log(result.values().join(","));` prints `3,1,2`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([3, 1]); const result = values.union(new Set<int>([1, 2])); console.log(result.values().join(","));
// prints 3,1,2
```

Ownership: both inputs borrow. This explicit result-producing operation copies selected keys, including owned text, into an independent Set. Binding or reading a Set never implicitly clones it.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([3, 1]); const result = values.union(new Set<int>([1, 2])); console.log(result.values().join(","));

Set.name: intersection
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent Set containing receiver keys also present in other. Takes exactly one Set; its key type may differ. Neither input is mutated. Results follow the insertion order of the smaller Set; ties use receiver order. Matching receiver keys are copied so the receiver key type is preserved. When numeric precision loss lets one other key match multiple exact receiver keys, all those receiver keys are retained. Empty inputs follow these same rules. Wrong arity, non-Set arguments and conflicting receiver mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Key comparisons retain existing native SameValueZero and enum identity rules. Large int/number overlap can lose precision. Union and symmetric difference infer a joined key type; intersection and difference keep the receiver key type.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.intersection(new Set<int>([2, 1])); console.log(result.values().join(","));` prints `2,1`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.intersection(new Set<int>([2, 1])); console.log(result.values().join(","));
// prints 2,1
```

Ownership: both inputs borrow. This explicit result-producing operation copies selected keys, including owned text, into an independent Set. Binding or reading a Set never implicitly clones it.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.intersection(new Set<int>([2, 1])); console.log(result.values().join(","));

Set.name: difference
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent Set containing receiver keys absent from other. Takes exactly one Set; its key type may differ. Neither input is mutated. Results follow receiver insertion order and preserve its key type. Empty inputs follow these same rules. Wrong arity, non-Set arguments and conflicting receiver mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Key comparisons retain existing native SameValueZero and enum identity rules. Large int/number overlap can lose precision. Union and symmetric difference infer a joined key type; intersection and difference keep the receiver key type.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.difference(new Set<int>([1, 2])); console.log(result.values().join(","));` prints `3`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.difference(new Set<int>([1, 2])); console.log(result.values().join(","));
// prints 3
```

Ownership: both inputs borrow. This explicit result-producing operation copies selected keys, including owned text, into an independent Set. Binding or reading a Set never implicitly clones it.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.difference(new Set<int>([1, 2])); console.log(result.values().join(","));

Set.name: symmetricDifference
Set.documentation:
Returns an independent Set containing keys present in exactly one input. Takes exactly one Set; its key type may differ. Neither input is mutated. Unshared receiver keys come first, followed by unshared other keys in their insertion order. Empty inputs follow these same rules. Wrong arity, non-Set arguments and conflicting receiver mutation/transfer during argument evaluation are static errors. Set-like records are not accepted.

Key comparisons retain existing native SameValueZero and enum identity rules. Large int/number overlap can lose precision. Union and symmetric difference infer a joined key type; intersection and difference keep the receiver key type.

Example: `const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.symmetricDifference(new Set<int>([2, 4, 1])); console.log(result.values().join(","));` prints `3,4`.

```tsrust
const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.symmetricDifference(new Set<int>([2, 4, 1])); console.log(result.values().join(","));
// prints 3,4
```

Ownership: both inputs borrow. This explicit result-producing operation copies selected keys, including owned text, into an independent Set. Binding or reading a Set never implicitly clones it.

examples.source: const values = new Set<int>([3, 1, 2]); const result = values.symmetricDifference(new Set<int>([2, 4, 1])); console.log(result.values().join(","));

Map.name: size
Map.documentation:
Returns the number of distinct keys. This property is readonly; assignment is rejected. It takes no arguments.

Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.size); // 1
```

Ownership: receiver is read and unchanged.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.size);

Map.name: set
Map.documentation:
Inserts a key and value, or replaces the value for an existing key. Replacement keeps the key’s original insertion position. Returns void; chaining is unsupported.

Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); values.set("a", 3); console.log(values.size, values.get("a") ?? 0); // 1 3
```

Ownership: owned keys and values transfer into the receiver; scalar inputs copy. Receiver mutates.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); values.set("a", 3); console.log(values.size, values.get("a") ?? 0);

Map.name: get
Map.documentation:
Reads the value for a key, or returns undefined when absent. Stored undefined remains distinguishable through has(). Receiver is unchanged.

Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.get("a") ?? 0, values.get("missing") ?? 0); // 1 0
```

Ownership: key is borrowed. Scalar values copy; owned values from a named receiver are readonly borrows and block mutation or transfer of that receiver while the borrow is in scope. A temporary receiver is consumed and its selected owned value moves out. Use clone() explicitly to own a copy of a borrowed value.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.get("a") ?? 0, values.get("missing") ?? 0);

Map.name: has
Map.documentation:
Reports whether a matching key exists, including when its stored value is undefined. Receiver is unchanged.

Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.has("a"), values.has("missing")); // true false
```

Ownership: receiver and key are borrowed.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.has("a"), values.has("missing"));

Map.name: delete
Map.documentation:
Removes a key and value and returns true, or returns false if absent. Remaining entries keep their order. Deleting and reinserting a key places it last.

Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.delete("a"), values.delete("a"), values.size); // true false 0
```

Ownership: key is borrowed; receiver mutates and the removed value is dropped.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); console.log(values.delete("a"), values.delete("a"), values.size);

Map.name: clear
Map.documentation:
Removes all entries and returns void. Takes no arguments.

Keys must match the declared key type. Scalar, enum and union keys are supported; record, array and function identity keys are unsupported. Number keys use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and both zeros are one key. Wrong argument counts or incompatible argument types are static errors.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); values.clear(); console.log(values.size); // 0
```

Ownership: receiver mutates; all keys and values are dropped.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>(); values.set("a", 1); values.clear(); console.log(values.size);

Map.name: keys

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>([["b", 2], ["a", 1]]); console.log(values.keys().join(","));

Map.documentation:
Returns an independent array of keys in insertion order. Takes no arguments and does not mutate the receiver. An empty Map returns an empty array. Replacement preserves the key position; deletion and reinsertion places it last. Later receiver changes do not change the snapshot. This operation returns an array snapshot, not a live iterator.

Example: `const values = new Map<string, int>([["b", 2], ["a", 1]]); console.log(values.keys().join(","));` prints `b,a`.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>([["b", 2], ["a", 1]]); console.log(values.keys().join(","));
// prints b,a
```

Ownership: Explicitly copies owned keys; the receiver stays usable.

Map.name: values

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>([["a", 1], ["b", 2], ["a", 3]]); console.log(values.values().join(","));

Map.documentation:
Returns an independent array of values in key insertion order. Takes no arguments and does not mutate the receiver. An empty Map returns an empty array. Replacement preserves the key position; deletion and reinsertion places it last. Later receiver changes do not change the snapshot. This operation returns an array snapshot, not a live iterator.

Example: `const values = new Map<string, int>([["a", 1], ["b", 2], ["a", 3]]); console.log(values.values().join(","));` prints `3,2`.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>([["a", 1], ["b", 2], ["a", 3]]); console.log(values.values().join(","));
// prints 3,2
```

Ownership: Explicitly copies owned values, including nested owned storage. Values must support cloning; the receiver stays usable.

Map.name: entries

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>([["a", 3]]); const pairs = values.entries(); console.log(pairs[0][0], pairs[0][1]);

Map.documentation:
Returns an independent array of key/value tuples in insertion order. Takes no arguments and does not mutate the receiver. An empty Map returns an empty array. Replacement preserves the key position; deletion and reinsertion places it last. Later receiver changes do not change the snapshot. This operation returns an array snapshot, not a live iterator.

Example: `const values = new Map<string, int>([["a", 3]]); const pairs = values.entries(); console.log(pairs[0][0], pairs[0][1]);` prints `a 3`.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>([["a", 3]]); const pairs = values.entries(); console.log(pairs[0][0], pairs[0][1]);
// prints a 3
```

Ownership: Explicitly copies owned keys and values into owned tuples. Values must support cloning; the receiver stays usable.

Map.signature: forEach(callback: (value: Value, key: Key, source: Map<Key, Value>) => Result): void
parameters: callback: (value: Value, key: Key, source: Map<Key, Value>) => Result
Map.documentation:
Calls a reusable callback once for each entry in insertion order. The callback receives the value, its key, and the readonly source Map. Replacing a key preserves its position; deletion and reinsertion places it last. An empty Map does not call the callback. Callbacks may use zero through three supplied positions; normal default and rest parameter rules apply. There is no thisArg argument. Wrong arity, incompatible parameter types/access, consuming callbacks, and receiver mutation or transfer during iteration are static errors.

Returns void and does not mutate the receiver. Each callback result is evaluated and discarded. A checked callback error stops iteration and propagates to surrounding catch/finally. External mutable captures are allowed when they do not conflict with receiver borrows.

Example: `const values = new Map<string, int>([["b", 2], ["a", 1]]); let text = ""; values.forEach((value, key) => { text = text + key + String(value) + "|"; }); console.log(text);` prints `b2|a1|`.

```tsrust
const values = new Map<string, int>([["b", 2], ["a", 1]]); let text = ""; values.forEach((value, key) => { text = text + key + String(value) + "|"; }); console.log(text);
// prints b2|a1|
```

Ownership: scalar keys and values copy; owned keys and values borrow readonly, as does the source Map. No owned callback input is implicitly cloned. Values need not support cloning.

examples.source: const values = new Map<string, int>([["b", 2], ["a", 1]]); let text = ""; values.forEach((value, key) => { text = text + key + String(value) + "|"; }); console.log(text);
